adults.title: When We Cannot Fix It
adults.big_idea: When we meet burdens we cannot carry ourselves, the Savior keeps His promise of peace by sending the Holy Ghost to comfort us.
adults.objective: Learners will name a burden they cannot fix alone, find the Savior's promises of comfort in the talk and the scriptures, and choose one way to draw nearer to Him and to the Holy Ghost this week.
prepare: Read Elder Matthew J. Eyring's talk, Comfort from the Holy Ghost, and mark paragraphs 2, 5, 6, 12 and 17.
Bring slips of paper and pencils for silent writing.
Write on the board: Draw near. Another Comforter. Mourn with those that mourn.
Pray by name for class members who are carrying something heavy. Do not plan to call on them; let them choose whether to speak.

segments.name: The thought that came
steps: Begin with prayer, and ask that the Holy Ghost will be the teacher and the comforter in the room.

Tell how the talk opens: a friend of Elder Eyring received a call from his wife telling him their young married son had passed away unexpectedly the night before. One thought came to his mind: “I can’t fix this.”
Hand out slips of paper. Invite everyone to write, silently and for no one else's eyes, one thing in their life right now that they cannot fix. Allow a full minute of quiet.
Say that no one will be asked to share what they wrote. Ask them to keep the paper in hand for the rest of the lesson.

segments.name: Burdens we cannot carry ourselves
steps: Read aloud the first key quote, from paragraph 2 of the talk.

Explain that Elder Eyring then lists burdens people carry: not enough food, failing health, loved ones who stray from the gospel path, hurting or being hurt by someone we love, loneliness, and a habit we have tried again and again to overcome. Read paragraph 5 if time allows.
Invite learners to turn to one person nearby and discuss the questions below for three minutes.
Ask one or two pairs to share a thought with the whole class.
questions: Why is it so hard for capable, faithful people to admit that a burden is too heavy to carry alone?
Elder Eyring says our self-reliance can mask a deeper reality. What have you learned when your own strength ran out?

segments.name: What the Savior promises
steps: Divide the class into groups of three or four. Give half the groups John 14:16–18 and the other half Doctrine and Covenants 88:63 with Alma 7:11–12.
Ask each group to read their verses aloud and list two things: what the Lord promises, and what He asks of us.
After four minutes, have each group report one promise. Write the promises on the board.

Read the second key quote, from paragraph 6. Point out what Elder Eyring adds: comfort and answers come on the Lord's timetable, and answers sometimes come as tools, resources, and help from other people.
Ask the questions below. Wait through the silence; let learners testify to one another.
questions: How is being comforted different from having the problem fixed?
When has the Holy Ghost comforted you in something that did not change, or did not change quickly?

segments.name: Comfort that comes through us
steps: Retell the dinner: Elder Eyring and his wife ate with a young couple who had lost one of their twins right before birth, in their first pregnancy. Many years earlier the Eyrings had gone through a similar loss. They talked together of parenthood, loss, and the path to healing and hope. Afterward Elder Eyring gave the father a priesthood blessing, and through the whisperings of the Spirit the father was promised peace. The couple left with their countenances shining.
Invite someone to read Mosiah 18:9 and find the covenant words Elder Eyring used to describe that evening.
Read the aligned quote about how God usually meets our needs: President Spencer W. Kimball's words, shared by President Eyring at this conference.
Discuss the questions below as a class.
questions: The Eyrings could not fix that couple's loss. What did they do instead?
Who has mourned with you in a way that let you feel the Lord's comfort? What did that person do, or wisely not do?

segments.name: There is hope in Jesus Christ
steps: Read the third key quote, from paragraph 12, and then President Oaks's words in the aligned quote.
Explain Elder Eyring's warning in paragraph 9: without divine comfort we risk losing hope, and without hope we can lose our faith and stop trying.
Check for understanding: ask learners to finish this sentence to a neighbor in their own words: Because of Jesus Christ, the thing I cannot fix is...

segments.name: Make room for the Comforter
steps: Read the last key quote, from paragraph 17.

Invite learners to turn over their slip of paper and write one specific thing they will do this week to draw near to the Lord and welcome the Holy Ghost, and the name of one person they could sit with in a hard time.
Remind them of the promise Elder Eyring quoted: “Draw near unto me and I will draw near unto you.”
Bear your own brief witness that Jesus Christ lives and does not leave us comfortless. Tell the class you will begin next week by asking who felt the Comforter during the week, and do it.

key_quotes.text: All of us, regardless of experience, talent, or willpower, will sooner or later encounter burdens we cannot possibly carry ourselves.
Our Savior, Jesus Christ, suffered for us. He knows exactly how we feel, especially in our darkest and most trying times.
Even as He comforts us through temporary times of challenge and pain, He has prepared our rescue from permanent tragedy.

The Savior’s peace is made manifest through the comforting power of the Holy Ghost. That comfort will help us when we go through the inevitable hardships of life and times when we can’t fix things on our own. Living worthy of the constant companionship of the Holy Ghost should be one of our highest priorities.

scriptures.use: Read in small groups. List what the Savior promises about the Comforter and how long that comfort is meant to stay.
Read in small groups with Alma 7:11–12. Name what the Lord asks of us and what He promises in return.
Read to see why the Savior knows exactly how we feel in our darkest times.
Read after the dinner story. Find the covenant words Elder Eyring used and ask how we keep them.

aligned_quotes.text: It gives us the strength and perspective to endure the mortal challenges faced by each of us and by those we love.
aligned_quotes.speaker: President Dallin H. Oaks
President Spencer W. Kimball, quoted by President Eyring
aligned_quotes.text: God does notice us, and he watches over us. But it is usually through another person that he meets our needs.

takeaways: Sooner or later every one of us meets a burden we cannot carry alone.
The Savior's peace reaches us through the comforting power of the Holy Ghost.
We keep our covenant when we mourn with those who mourn, even when we cannot fix anything.
act: Each day this week, pray about the thing you wrote down and tell the Lord plainly that you cannot fix it alone. Notice any comfort that comes and write it down.
Choose one thing that crowds the Holy Ghost out of your day and set it aside for the week. Put in its place one thing that invites Him.
Sit with one person who is hurting. Listen more than you speak, and do not try to fix it.
If you are carrying a burden in silence, consider asking for a priesthood blessing.
music: Where Can I Turn for Peace?
adapt: At home or with two or three people: skip the groups. Read John 14:16–18 together and let each person answer one question from the third segment.
Large class: keep every discussion in pairs or threes so that all speak, and take only two comments from the whole room each time.
Short on time: teach segments 1, 3 and 6. The silent writing and the promise in Doctrine and Covenants 88:63 carry the lesson.

youth.title: Not Everything Can Be Fixed. Everything Can Be Comforted.
youth.big_idea: Some problems are too big for us to fix, and the Savior sends the Holy Ghost to comfort us and give us hope while we go through them.
youth.objective: Youth will be able to explain in their own words how the Savior comforts us through the Holy Ghost, and will choose one way to invite the Spirit and one way to comfort a friend this week.
prepare: Read Elder Matthew J. Eyring's talk, Comfort from the Holy Ghost, especially paragraphs 1–2, 6 and 17.

Write eight problems on separate slips of paper: a cracked phone screen, a failed test, a messy room, a friend who is moving away, a grandparent who is very sick, feeling lonely at school, an argument with a brother or sister, a habit I keep going back to.
On the board make two columns: I can fix this. I can't fix this alone.
Bring paper and pens. Ask youth to have their scriptures or the Gospel Library app ready.

segments.name: Fix it or not
steps: As youth walk in, hand each one a slip and have them stick or set it under one of the two columns on the board. No explanation yet.
Once the slips are up, invite an opening prayer.
Ask the group to challenge any slip they think is in the wrong column. Let them argue briefly; several slips belong in both.
Ask the question below, and take two or three quick answers.
questions: What is different about the problems in the second column?

segments.name: A phone call
steps: Tell how the talk begins. A friend of Elder Eyring got a call from his wife: their young married son had unexpectedly passed away the night before. He said one thought came to his mind: “I can’t fix this.”
Have a youth read the first key quote, from paragraph 2.
Ask the questions below. Be gentle; some in the room may be living in the second column right now. No one has to share anything personal.
questions: We are taught to solve problems and be strong. Why might Elder Eyring say that is not the whole picture?
What do people your age usually do with a problem they cannot fix? What helps, and what only hides it for a while?

segments.name: Promise hunt
steps: Make three teams. Assign one passage to each: Doctrine and Covenants 88:63, John 14:16–18, and Philippians 4:7.
Each team has three minutes to read its verses and write the Lord's promise in six words or fewer, in their own words, on a sheet of paper.
Teams hold up their sheets and read them. Let everyone vote, with eyes closed and a raised hand, for the clearest one that is not their own.
Read the second key quote, from paragraph 6, and ask which team's promise it matches best.
Ask the question below.
questions: John 14 calls the Holy Ghost a Comforter. Why do you think the Savior chose that name for Him?

segments.name: What if I don't feel anything?
steps: Say that this is an honest question and that many faithful people ask it.

Have youth scan paragraph 6 of the talk on their phones and find what Elder Eyring says about when and how comfort and answers come. They should find that the Lord answers on His timetable, and that answers sometimes come as tools, resources, and help from other people.
Read Elder Kearon's words in the aligned quotes, then Elder Dunn's.
In pairs, have youth answer the first question below. Then ask the second question to the whole group and share an experience of your own if it is fitting.
questions: If comfort from the Spirit is not always words, what else can it be like?
When has peace or help come to you through another person, a scripture, or a quiet feeling, even though the problem was still there?

segments.name: Be someone's comfort
steps: Briefly tell about the dinner. Elder Eyring and his wife ate with a young couple whose baby, one of twins, had died right before birth. The Eyrings had been through a similar loss many years before. They did not fix anything. They listened, talked about loss and hope, and Elder Eyring gave the father a priesthood blessing that promised him peace.
Have someone read Mosiah 18:9 and find the two things we promise at baptism that the Eyrings did that night.

Role play in pairs. One person is a friend whose week has fallen apart (keep it made up and general). The other has one minute to respond without giving advice and without trying to fix it. Then switch.
Ask the question below.
questions: What did your partner say or do that actually helped? What would you leave out next time?

segments.name: Make it a priority
steps: Read the third key quote, from paragraph 17. Point out that Elder Eyring calls living worthy of the Spirit one of our highest priorities.
Silent writing, on paper or in a phone note: one thing this week that pushes the Spirit out of my day, one thing I will do to invite Him, and one person I will check on.
Check for understanding: ask two volunteers to explain in one sentence how the Savior comforts us when we cannot fix something.

Share the promise Elder Eyring quoted: “Draw near unto me and I will draw near unto you.” Testify that there is hope in Jesus Christ. Tell the youth you will ask next week what they noticed, and then ask.

key_quotes.text: All of us, regardless of experience, talent, or willpower, will sooner or later encounter burdens we cannot possibly carry ourselves.
He knows exactly how we feel, especially in our darkest and most trying times.

That comfort will help us when we go through the inevitable hardships of life and times when we can’t fix things on our own. Living worthy of the constant companionship of the Holy Ghost should be one of our highest priorities.
There is hope in Jesus Christ.

scriptures.use: Team one reads it and writes the Lord's promise in six words or fewer.
Team two reads it and writes the promise in six words or fewer; then discuss why the Holy Ghost is called a Comforter.
Team three reads it and writes the promise in six words or fewer.
Read before the role play. Find the two things we promise to do for people who are hurting.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Kearon
aligned_quotes.text: The language of the Spirit of God is not a language of words.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Dunn
aligned_quotes.text: Peace will come even when hoped-for outcomes do not.

takeaways: Some things I cannot fix, and that is not a failure of faith.
The Savior knows exactly how I feel, and He sends the Holy Ghost to comfort me.
I can be part of the Lord's comfort for a friend by showing up and listening.
act: Pick one second-column problem in your life. Pray about it by name every day this week and tell the Lord you cannot fix it alone.
For seven days, trade ten minutes of scrolling for ten quiet minutes with the scriptures or a conference talk, and notice how you feel.
Message or sit with one person who is having a hard time. Do not give advice. Just be there.
At the end of each day, write one line in your phone about any moment of peace you noticed.
music: Where Can I Turn for Peace?
adapt: At home or with one or two youth: do the sorting slips together on a table, give each person one promise passage, and do the role play as a family.
Large class: make six teams for the promise hunt, two per passage, and compare the two versions of each promise.
Short on time: do segments 1, 3 and 6. If someone in the group is grieving, skip the role play and spend that time on Mosiah 18:9.

children.title: The Holy Ghost Comforts Me
children.big_idea: When I am sad or scared, Jesus sends the Holy Ghost to comfort me.
children.objective: Children will be able to say that the Holy Ghost comforts them and will name one thing they can do when they feel sad or scared: pray to Heavenly Father.
prepare: Read Elder Matthew J. Eyring's talk, Comfort from the Holy Ghost, especially the last two paragraphs.
Bring a soft blanket, a bag or backpack filled with a few heavy books, paper, and crayons.
Be ready to sing The Holy Ghost. Children who do not know it can hum or listen.

segments.name: Welcome and song
steps: Greet each child by name. Invite a child to pray.
Sing The Holy Ghost together, or A Child's Prayer if the children know it better.
Teach the sentence for today and have the children say it with you three times, first in a whisper, then in a speaking voice, then with a hand over the heart: The Holy Ghost comforts me.

segments.name: Too heavy for one
steps: Set the heavy bag on the floor. Let one or two children try to lift it with one hand. Keep it light enough that no one can be hurt.
Ask a second child to help, and lift it together. Then help them yourself.
Say: Elder Eyring taught that everyone, even grown-ups, will have things that are too heavy to carry alone. He did not mean bags. He meant feelings like being very sad, scared, or lonely.
Ask the question below, and thank each child who answers.
questions: What does it feel like when someone helps you with something that is too heavy?

segments.name: The Comforter
steps: Hold up the blanket. Ask what a blanket does for us when we are cold or tired.
Explain that Jesus promised His friends He would send a Comforter to stay with them. The Comforter is the Holy Ghost. We cannot see Him, but He can help us feel peaceful and loved inside.
Pass the blanket around the circle. Each child wraps it around their shoulders for a moment and says: The Holy Ghost comforts me.
Say: A blanket warms the outside of us. The Holy Ghost comforts the inside of us.

segments.name: A story from the talk
steps: Tell the story simply. Elder Eyring and his wife went to dinner with a young husband and wife who were very sad because something very hard had happened in their family. Elder Eyring and his wife had once felt that same kind of sadness, so they understood. They sat at the table, listened, and talked about hope.

Continue: After dinner Elder Eyring gave the father a priesthood blessing. In the blessing the Holy Ghost whispered that the father would have peace. When the couple went home, their faces were shining with the light of Jesus.
Act it out. Choose children to sit at a pretend table and listen kindly to one another. Have everyone show a sad face, then a peaceful face.
Ask the questions below.
questions: Who helped the mother and father feel peace?
How can we help someone who is sad?

segments.name: Draw near
steps: Stand at one side of the room and have the children line up at the other.
Tell them Jesus made a promise: when we come closer to Him, He comes closer to us.

Name ways we draw near to Jesus, one at a time: I pray. I sing a Primary song. I listen to the scriptures. I am kind. Each time, the children take one step toward you and you take one step toward them.
When you meet in the middle, say together: The Holy Ghost comforts me.

segments.name: Draw and tell
steps: Give each child paper and crayons.
Invite them to draw themselves praying at a time when they feel sad or scared. They may draw the blanket around their shoulders to remind them of the Comforter.
As they draw, move from child to child and ask each one to tell you about the picture.
Help each child write or trace at the top: The Holy Ghost comforts me.

segments.name: Jesus's promise
steps: Gather the children close. Open your scriptures to John 14:18 and read the promise Elder Eyring shared at the end of his talk: “I will not leave you comfortless: I will come to you.”
Check for understanding: ask, Who comforts us? What can we do when we are sad or scared? Listen for the Holy Ghost and for praying.
Have the children repeat after you the words Elder Fale said at this conference (see the aligned quote). Bear a short witness that Jesus Christ lives.
Invite them to pray this week whenever they feel sad or scared, and to show their picture to someone at home. Tell them you will ask about it next week. Close with prayer.

key_quotes.text: There is hope in Jesus Christ.
I will not leave you comfortless: I will come to you.
The Savior’s peace is made manifest through the comforting power of the Holy Ghost.

scriptures.use: Read aloud from your scriptures in the closing segment as Jesus's promise to each child.
Use in the blanket activity: tell the children in your own words that Jesus promised to send a Comforter to stay with us.
The idea behind the stepping game. Older children can read it aloud before the game begins.

aligned_quotes.speaker: Elder Fale
aligned_quotes.text: I am a child of God and He loves me.

takeaways: When I am sad or scared, I can pray to Heavenly Father.
Jesus promised He will not leave me without comfort.
act: Pray to Heavenly Father when you feel sad or scared this week.
Put your picture where you will see it at bedtime.
When you see someone who is sad, sit by them and be kind.

adapt.younger: Ages 3–7: shorten the story to three sentences and let the children hold the blanket while you tell it. Repeat the stepping game twice, since they will ask for it. Use helpers to lift the bag and to pass the blanket. Say the sentence The Holy Ghost comforts me after every activity.
adapt.older: Ages 8–11: have one child read John 14:18 and another read Doctrine and Covenants 88:63 aloud. Let an older child lead the stepping game and choose the ways we draw near. Ask a harder question: How can the Holy Ghost comfort us even when the hard thing does not go away? Invite them to write one sentence under their drawing about a time they felt peace.
